title: Polynomial-time detection of fixed pivot- and vertex-minors
formal: For each relation \(\rho\in\{\text{pivot-minor},\text{vertex-minor}\}\) and each fixed finite simple graph \(H\), does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, on every finite simple graph \(G\), decides whether some \(\rho\) of \(G\) is isomorphic to \(H\)?
why: Efficient fixed-pattern detection would make local-transformation graph structure algorithmically accessible, with consequences for graph classes and graph-state transformations.

textbook_notes.summary: Detect any fixed pivot-minor or vertex-minor in polynomial time.
textbook_notes.status_note: Presented in the cited 2016 source version. The import does not verify present open status; this dated note does not override a later card review.

category_assignment.reason: The requested result is a polynomial-time containment algorithm, rather than a structural theorem about excluded minors.

importance.reason: A general algorithmic counterpart to structural graph containment, connecting width theory with transformations used in quantum graph states.

sentences: The target is to detect a fixed graph after specified local graph transformations and vertex deletions.
Vertex-minors permit local complementation, while pivot-minors permit the more restricted edge-pivot operation.
The host graph is arbitrary and the target’s vertices may be placed anywhere.
For each fixed target and relation, one deterministic algorithm must run in polynomial time in host size.
The question does not require a common polynomial exponent or a uniform algorithm for all target sizes.

definitions: Graphs are finite, undirected, loopless and have no parallel edges. Local complementation at a vertex \(v\) toggles adjacency between each pair of distinct neighbors of \(v\), leaving all other adjacencies unchanged. If \(uv\) is an edge in the current graph, pivoting on \(uv\) means local complementation at \(u\), then \(v\), then \(u\). A vertex-minor is obtained by a finite sequence of local complementations and vertex deletions; a pivot-minor instead permits edge pivots and vertex deletions. A deletion removes the chosen vertex and all its incident edges. Isomorphism is a bijection preserving adjacency in both directions; target vertices have no prescribed locations in the host. The empty target is allowed. For each fixed pair \((\rho,H)\), the algorithm receives only \(G\), encoded by its vertex count and adjacency matrix in binary. There must be constants \(C_{\rho,H},a_{\rho,H}>0\) such that it always returns the correct bit in at most \(C_{\rho,H}(n+1)^{a_{\rho,H}}\) Turing steps on every \(n\)-vertex host. Its program and these constants may depend on the fixed target and relation. No uniform construction from an input \(H\), fixed-parameter bound, containment witness or host-width promise is required. There is no advice depending on the growing host.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of the quantified polynomial-time decision algorithms for both relations and every fixed target, or a Lean refutation for some fixed target and relation. A result only for hosts of bounded width or a bound exponential in host size does not meet the assertion. A uniform fixed-parameter algorithm would be sufficient but is not required.

context_blocks.text: Local complementation and edge pivoting define graph containment relations that differ from ordinary edge-contraction minors. The source asks whether fixed targets can be recognized efficiently in arbitrary hosts.
The 2024 survey repeats fixed-target vertex-minor detection as Conjecture 14.1. Its following conjecture concerns specified target vertices, a different formulation.
